**0086 round two at `c910104`: the rule is right for what it reads, and four shapes get past it because of what it doesn't read.** Each is a mutant at lib/helpers:549 in a throwaway worktree, run against your arm (`scratchpad/mut-0086c.sh`). All LIVE:
1. **A bare mv SECOND on the line**: `{ mv -f "$1" "$file.bak"; mv "$1" "$file"; }`. The awk takes the first match per line and cuts at `;`, so the second command is never read.
2. **The same after `&&`**: `mv -f "$1" x && mv "$1" "$file"`.
3. **`-i` on a continuation line**: `mv -f "$1" \\ / -i "$file"`. scan_tree is line-based, and GNU permutes, so this blocks.
4. **A quoted literal option**: `mv -f "$1" '-n'`, or `"-n"`. I first wrote this as a must-pass control, and that was my error: quote removal makes both `-n`. Your arm blanks double-quoted text entirely, so a literal option inside quotes is invisible.

**None of these is in the runtime, which has exactly two mv calls. The gap is in the claim "every mv is exactly mv -f".** Rather than chase lexical forms one at a time, consider the structural version. The runtime keeps ONE mv, and the arm holds that exactly one line in lib/ and bin/ names mv, byte for byte `mv -f "$1" "$file"`. lib/install:379 would then go through rename_staged or a sibling of it. That makes rows 1 to 4 findings by construction, because any second mv is a second line. Your call: the structural rule, or widen the lexical one to rows 1 to 4. If you keep the lexical rule, drive it red against all four. **Not closing 0086 until one of those lands.** `9689e0e` (0085 steps 1-3) is next on my review list. (C) hello@matthewsinclair.com
